clue.text: Slightly more detailed clothes for one in a sequined costume

indicators.note: used as a verb: the trimmed word dresses, wraps around, the other piece
with its tail cut off, so the last letter of the word more goes

parts.note: a tad means slightly, a little bit

explanation.surface: A remark that a sparkly outfit is a little more elaborate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' looks like 'elaborate' but means de-tailed, losing the last letter; 'clothes' is a verb, wrapping one piece around the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A bullfighter famously wears the glittering suit of lights, a sequined costume.

clue.text: Club with a scheme to prepare a strip of beef?

definitions.note: a strip is a stretch of shore and beef is brawn, so a beach famed for brawny bodybuilders

indicators.note: preparing something means working it into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A golf or sports club plans how to cut a strip of beef.
explanation.walkthrough: MUSCLE BEACH is the bodybuilding beachfront at Venice, California; 'beef' is slang for muscle and 'strip' a stretch of sand.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: beefy bodybuilders gather on that stretch of seafront sand.

clue.text: Scrawny geezer, less posh — I don't recall his name

parts.note: scrawny means thin

indicators.note: signals taking away, here the letter for posh

parts.note: a geezer is British slang for a guy, a bloke
U is the old abbreviation for upper-class, posh

explanation.surface: Someone describes a thin, rather common man whose name escapes them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'geezer' is British slang for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: A word used as a placeholder for a person or object whose name has slipped the mind.

clue.text: Current housing is heading for trouble, so upset

indicators.note: holding inside, so the draught contains the other pieces

parts.note: a current of air is a draught
taken as written

indicators.note: the head, the first letter, of the word trouble

explanation.surface: An electric current at home is causing trouble, so someone is upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' suggests electricity, but here it is a current of air, a DRAUGHT, holding IS and T.
explanation.definitionFit: Being upset in the sense of very distressed or agitated.

clue.text: Second paper, one among the others

indicators.note: placed among, inside, the other letters

parts.note: the rest means the others
the Roman numeral I is one

explanation.surface: A second exam paper is set, one among several others.
explanation.definitionFit: An exam taken again after failing is a second sitting of a paper.

clue.text: Is one too tired for the Listener?

definitions.text: Is one too tired for the Listener?

parts.words: Is one too tired for the Listener?
parts.note: to a listener 'too tired' sounds like 'two-tyred', having a pair of tyres, which describes a pushbike

explanation.definitionFit: A pedal machine runs on a pair of tyres, so it is a two-tyred vehicle.

clue.text: Bitter dough?

parts.note: bitter is a British beer and dough is slang for money, so cash set aside for drinks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter' looks like an adjective, but is the British pale ale; 'dough' is slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Pocket cash for drinks; the phrase also means small spare money for minor treats.

clue.text: Diminutive reptile buried in volcanic rock

indicators.note: the letters lie buried inside the run of the words volcanic rock

explanation.surface: A tiny lizard is entombed in lava stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortened, diminutive form of the name for a large river-dwelling reptile.

clue.text: Front (not middle) to drop, with modest coat finely spun

indicators.note: used as a verb: the modest word covers the other pieces

parts.note: coy means shy, modest

indicators.note: removing the central letter of the word for the front

parts.note: the bow is the front of a ship
to ebb is to fall away, drop

explanation.surface: A garment front dropped, with a plain coat of delicate weave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front' is a ship's front; 'not middle' drops its central letter, and 'coat' is a verb, the shy word covering the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Like the delicate threads a spider weaves, thin and gossamer-fine.

clue.text: Always before involving the state, testament erased

indicators.note: wrapping around, so the old word for before contains the rest

parts.note: ere is an old word for before

indicators.note: taken out, so those letters go from the state's name

parts.note: a US state, here Vermont
NT is the New Testament

explanation.surface: Something lasting forever, from before the state existed, with its testament wiped out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the state' is the US state of Vermont; 'erased' takes out the abbreviation for New Testament, and 'involving' wraps the old word for before around what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic or old-fashioned word meaning for all time.

clue.text: Cuckoo clocks, chocolates, snow, Alps and Heidi ultimately — this?

definitions.text: Cuckoo clocks, chocolates, snow, Alps and Heidi ultimately — this?

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so the letters are scrambled
take the final letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A list of national clichés: cuckoo clocks, chocolates, snow, mountains and the girl Heidi — what nation is this?
explanation.walkthrough: The last letters are S S W S I; 'Cuckoo' rearranges them. The whole clue lists famous emblems of one country, so it defines too.
explanation.definitionFit: Each item listed is a stock emblem of Switzerland, so the nationality fits.

clue.text: Identify large drink — and be affected by it?

parts.note: to see something is to identify it
a double is a twice-sized measure of spirits

explanation.surface: Someone spots a big drink and feels its effects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' refers back to the large drink: too much leaves one with blurred vision.
explanation.definitionFit: Drunkenness causes blurred double vision, an effect of too much alcohol.

clue.text: Napier's figures almost right, not entirely wrong

indicators.note: the letters are put wrongly, rearranged
the word right is not used in full, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A complaint that Napier's numbers were nearly right and partly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: John Napier, Scottish mathematician, invented these tables. RIGH plus ALMOST are scrambled by 'wrong'.
explanation.definitionFit: John Napier devised these mathematical tables of exponents in 1614.

clue.text: Some light, or heavy, supporting structure

definitions.meaning: a shaft or ray of light
a large timber or girder holding up a building

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a ray of sunlight and a heavy horizontal girder in building.

clue.text: Rubbish bin arrives as area emptying the water

indicators.note: used as a verb, rubbishing letters scrambles them

explanation.surface: A rubbish bin turns up as the area is cleared of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A drainage region whose streams carry water off into a main channel.

clue.text: Barely trendy big but not good musician, losing head as superstar

parts.note: just means barely, only just
in means fashionable

indicators.note: the word big minus the letter for good
the composer's name drops its first letter

parts.note: Carl Maria von Weber, the German composer

explanation.surface: A barely trendy, overblown performer loses his top billing as a star.
explanation.walkthrough: BIG loses G to give BI; WEBER, the composer, loses W to give EBER.
explanation.definitionFit: The Canadian singer is a pop megastar with a huge worldwide following.

clue.text: Stop Britartist installing the first bit of rubbish in gallery

indicators.note: placed inside the gallery's name

parts.note: the Tate is a London art gallery

indicators.note: putting inside, so the artist's name holds the letter

parts.note: Tracey Emin is a famous Young British Artist

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word rubbish

explanation.surface: Halt the artist putting rubbish into a gallery, an allusion to Emin's notorious unmade bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Tracey Emin is a Britartist known for her unmade bed exhibit; the Tate is a London gallery. 'installing' and 'in' both signal one piece going inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring to an end, halt or stop something.

clue.text: Dowdiest sort of paper like this

definitions.note: describes a newspaper, printed on both faces, rather than naming it

indicators.note: to sort letters is to arrange them, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: This newspaper is a rather drab sort of thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paper like this' describes the newspaper you hold, printed on both faces, so the answer is an adjective for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Newsprint carries text on both faces, front and back, so it has a pair of faces.

clue.text: Measure in computer language left smoke, in the words of Keats, to rise

indicators.note: in a down light, rising means reading upwards, backwards
these letters go inside the verse

parts.note: a poem by the poet John Keats
fag is British slang for a cigarette

explanation.surface: A computing measure: smoke drifting upward, as Keats might have described it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smoke' is the British slang word for a cigarette; 'in' puts left and smoke inside the verse, and 'to rise' reads the whole upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of computing speed: a million floating-point operations per second.

clue.text: Picture dork eating chicken with badger on the side in New York

indicators.note: taking inside, so the fool's word contains the rest

parts.note: a wally is British slang for a fool
a hen is a chicken
to harry is to pester or badger
the Mets are a New York baseball team

explanation.surface: A fool eats chicken with a pestering animal beside him in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badger' looks like the animal but is the verb meaning pester; WALLY is British slang for a twit. The Mets are a baseball side.
explanation.definitionFit: Picture is slang for a film, and this is a 1989 romantic comedy movie.

clue.text: Chopper in man, pronounced

indicators.note: says the word aloud, giving the spelling in the grid

parts.note: a fella is a man

explanation.surface: A helicopter carrying a man, as said aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chopper' suggests a helicopter but is one who chops trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodcutter is someone who fells trees.

clue.text: As hair without bleach revived, might you say?

indicators.note: signals the sound of the word rather than its spelling

parts.note: brought back to life, no longer dead, so 'un-died'

explanation.surface: A question about natural hair coming back to life.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair untouched by colouring or bleaching keeps its natural shade.

clue.text: See 24
Paul's wife in cutie snatched by virtually mad African

indicators.note: taken into the grip of the outer word
almost all of it, the last letter dropping

parts.note: zany means crazy, mad
Paul is the setter, so Paul's is I am, I'M

indicators.note: placed inside the next word

parts.note: a babe is an attractive person, a cutie

explanation.surface: The setter's wife, a cutie, is snatched by a crazed man from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paul' is this puzzle's setter, so 'Paul's' reads as I'M. ZANY loses Y to give ZAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from the country in southern Africa whose capital is Harare.

clue.text: See 1
Years of being in pain, self-destructive

indicators.note: destroying letters breaks them up for rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone spends years in pain, bent on hurting themself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'self-destructive' reads as one word, but splits: SELF is fodder and 'destructive' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The length of time a living thing exists, its years alive.

clue.text: A boy heading west, a country being taken over, leader in exile

indicators.note: in an across clue, westward means read backwards

parts.note: a lad is a boy

indicators.note: turned over, so read in reverse

parts.note: Mali is a West African country

explanation.surface: A boy travels west as a country is conquered by a leader who has fled.
explanation.walkthrough: A LAD reversed gives DALA; A MALI reversed gives ILAMA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tibetan spiritual head has lived abroad in India since 1959.

clue.text: See 18
Cut round opening in pine to get sap

indicators.note: the word for cut goes around the letter

parts.note: to delete is to cut out text

indicators.note: the first letter of the word pine

explanation.surface: Slashing round a pine tree to draw out its sap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sap' looks like tree resin, but is the verb to drain or weaken.
explanation.definitionFit: To sap is to drain or exhaust, use up.

clue.text: Dog missing old wine a ton

indicators.note: without, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a hound is a dog
red is red wine

explanation.surface: A dog lacking old wine by the ton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a ton' is British slang for a hundred, as in a hundred pounds or a century in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A ton is British slang for one hundred, of runs, pounds or miles per hour.
